introduction: Detachment, the first of these readings says, is as the sun: where it shines it quenches the fire of covetousness and self. What follows is a long instruction in letting go, of possessions, praise and blame, the homeland of this world and finally the self, with patience as the steed of the journey and a series of prayers asking to be rid of all attachment to any but God. The Gospels, the Qur’an, the Psalms, the Dhammapada, the Gītā, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius and Thomas à Kempis keep the readings close company. The dissent is as old. The Preacher and Herrick conclude from the shortness of life that its goods should be enjoyed; Tagore finds freedom in a thousand bonds of delight; Milton will not praise a cloistered virtue, nor Donne an island; Mencius defends the ties of kin; Thoreau hears desperation under the word resignation; and Ivan Karamazov returns the ticket.
questions: Bahá’u’lláh writes that true reliance is to pursue one’s calling in this world while holding fast to the Lord, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that building is praiseworthy if one is not attached to what is built. How do Paul’s “use this world, as not abusing it” and the Qur’an’s “neglect not thy portion of the world” help in saying what detachment is not?

The Preacher, Herrick and Khayyám start from the same passing of time as the readings and reach enjoyment, not renunciation. What in the readings would answer them, and what in them deserves to be kept?

“Shut the door of friendship and enmity upon all the people of the earth”; “no man is an island”. How can both be true of the same seeker, given what the readings elsewhere say about service and nearness to God?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that he was happier in prison because he had no will of his own; Thoreau says that what is called resignation is confirmed desperation; Shakespeare puts the praise of patience in Iago’s mouth. By what signs would you tell the patience these readings mean from its counterfeits?

The prayers ask to be severed from every tie but the tie to those who cleave to God. How do Jesus’ saying about his mother and brothers, the Qur’an’s list of what is held dearer than God, and Mencius’s defence of father and prince bear on that request?
Ben Zoma calls rich the one who rejoices in his lot; the prayers ask to be made rich enough to dispense with all but God. Are these the same wealth?

outside.why: The one who understands “will assuredly detach himself from the world and the vanities thereof”. The First Epistle of John gives the charge and its reason: the world passeth away, and the lust thereof.
Detachment “quencheth the fire of covetousness and self”. Emerson describes the fire unquenched, in his own prosperous country: things are in the saddle, and ride mankind.
Detachment means that “neither love of anything nor occupation with it should veil one from divine love”. Jesus puts the same exclusiveness as a matter of service: no man can serve two masters.

“True reliance is for the servant to pursue his profession and calling in this world, to hold fast unto the Lord.” The Qur’an keeps both halves in one verse: seek the Hereafter, and neglect not thy portion of the world.
“If the whole earth were to be converted into silver and gold”, the one who has ascended would not regard it. In the Gospel the whole earth is actually offered, from a high mountain, and refused.
“Neither give ear to commendation and praise, nor be saddened or heartbroken by censure.” Kipling’s advice to a son treats triumph and disaster the same way, as two impostors.

“Be not saddened by the sorrows of the world, nor gladdened by its joys.” The Qur’an gives the same pair as the purpose of knowing that all is written: that ye grieve not for what escaped you, nor exult in what is given.

“Though the mind is busy, the heart must be attracted toward the Kingdom.” Martha’s mind is busy and she is gently told that one thing is needful, which her sister has chosen. Does the reading side with Mary, or describe a third way that Luke’s story leaves out?
“An earthly edifice, even if raised as high as the heavens, will ultimately become a ruin.” Shelley’s traveller reports what is left of a king of kings: two legs of stone and the level sands.

Building palaces “is acceptable and praiseworthy”, only “one should not become attached to them”. Paul’s formula for the same balance is to use this world as not abusing it, for its fashion passes away.
“Turn thy face unto Mine and renounce all save Me.” The psalmist has reached that point by himself: whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.

“The sign of love is fortitude under My decree and patience under My trials.” Job gives the sign in a sentence, and keeps his right to argue in the same breath: though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.
“Cast away that which ye possess, and, on the wings of detachment, soar.” Jesus makes it the condition of discipleship: whoever forsakes not all that he has cannot be my disciple.

The reading would have its hearers “soar beyond all created things”. Tagore, a devout poet, refuses that road: deliverance is not for me in renunciation; I feel the embrace of freedom in a thousand bonds of delight. Can the created things be the way and not the weight?
“Forsake all that ye possess, and enter beneath the shadow of your Lord.” The young man who is told to sell what he has and follow goes away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.
“Better is this for you than all your works of the past and of the future.” Paul reckons his own past works the same way: what things were gain to me, those I counted loss.

“Forsake all that ye possess.” The Preacher, who has also seen that everything passes, concludes that it is good and comely to eat and drink and enjoy the good of one’s labour, for it is one’s portion. Which conclusion follows from the shortness of life?
Blessed is the one “whom the things of the world have not kept back” from the Court. In the parable a man sells all that he has for joy, because of what is in the field.
“The hours and moments of your lives have come and gone … Even as the swiftness of lightning your days shall pass.” The psalm asks for the use of that knowledge: teach us to number our days.

Time is flying, says the reading; therefore detach yourselves from what perishes. Herrick starts from the same flying time and draws the opposite moral: gather ye rosebuds while ye may. What decides between them?
“All tombs and sepulchres, even of the world’s most celebrated monarchs, are dark and gloomy.” Gray, in a village churchyard: the paths of glory lead but to the grave.
“Be thou severed from this world, and reborn.” Paul to the Colossians: set your affection on things above; for ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.
“Build ye for yourselves such houses as the rain and floods can never destroy.” The Sermon on the Mount ends on that house: the rain descended and the floods came, and it fell not.
Those created in this day “will cast the world and all that is therein behind”. The Epistle to the Hebrews tells it of Moses, who refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter.

“Whoso hath partaken of the wine of His remembrance will forget every other remembrance.” Khayyám, in FitzGerald’s English, knows another wine and another forgetting, and calls the wilderness with it “Paradise enow”. Are the two wines rivals, or is one a figure of the other?
The wise man “at some moments, even … eagerly wisheth for death that he may thereby be freed”. Paul in prison weighs the same wish and stays: to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

The wise man, says the reading, does not attach himself to this mortal life. Tennyson’s old king thinks it dull to pause and rust unburnished, and wants more of life, not less. Is his appetite the attachment the reading means?
“Beware lest the might of any oppressor frighten you. Soon shall the banners and standards perish.” The second psalm watches the kings of the earth set themselves, and hears laughter in heaven.
“Make not the world your homeland.” The Epistle to the Hebrews: here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.

The reading sets a homeland of the All-Merciful against this world. Jesus, praying for his disciples, asks something more exact: not that they be taken out of the world, but kept from the evil. What is the difference between leaving the world and not making it one’s home?
“Ye should renounce existence and non-existence, light and darkness, glory and abasement alike.” The Dhammapada is as thorough: give up what is before, what is behind, what is in the middle.
Souls “who will consign their own selves to oblivion” attain real union. The Gospel’s paradox: whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it.
“Blessed art thou for having utterly abolished the idol of self.” The Dhammapada ranks that victory above a thousand battles: he who conquers himself is the greatest of conquerors.

Nearness to God is possible, says ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, through “service to humanity” and “unity with mankind” as well as severance. Milton could not praise a virtue that never sallies out to meet its adversary. How does severance differ from the cloister he distrusts?

Covetousness is the first of “the three things that must be renounced”. The First Letter to Timothy gives the plain reason: we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.
“Let us neither make known our sufferings nor complain of our wrongs.” Marcus Aurelius tells himself to be like the promontory against which the waves continually break.
To be detached from self is to “yield up the self and all its concerns on the field of martyrdom”. Jesus: let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.
“Do all ye can to become wholly weary of self, and bind yourselves to that Countenance.” John the Baptist, when his followers leave him for another: he must increase, but I must decrease.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá guards against a misreading: self-forgetting does not mean that one “should allow his physical health to deteriorate”. Paul’s words about keeping his body under have fed the ascetic reading for centuries. Where does discipline of the self end and harm to the body begin?

“Strive only to be obedient and submissive to the Will of God. In this way only shall we become citizens of the Kingdom.” A soul in Dante’s lowest heaven says why she wants no higher place: his will is our peace.

“Leave all thought of self.” Polonius’s parting counsel, which the modern world has taken as its creed, is to be true above all to thine own self. Which self is the reading leaving, and which is Polonius keeping?
“The veil of covetousness” on the inner eye shuts out everything. The rich man of the parable sees only his barns and his many years, and is called a fool the same night.
“The steed of this valley is patience; without patience the wayfarer on this journey will reach nowhere.” Jesus, of harder times than a search: in your patience possess ye your souls.
The seeker sets out through the Valley of Search with nothing but patience. Bunyan’s dreamer sees a man setting out too, with a book in his hand and a great burden on his back.

“If he strive for a hundred thousand years and yet fail to behold the beauty of the Friend, he should not falter.” Milton, blind at forty-four and afraid of being useless: they also serve who only stand and wait.
The seeker must “turn away from imitation, which is following the traces of their forefathers”. The Qur’an quotes the reply this meets: we follow that wherein we found our fathers.

The seeker is to “shut the door of friendship and enmity upon all the people of the earth”. Donne, on his sickbed, finds that no man is an island, entire of itself. What kind of door is the reading closing, if Donne is right?
“Free thyself from the fetters of blind imitation.” Emerson says that the conviction arrives in every education: envy is ignorance, imitation is suicide.
The knower flings himself into the sea; the grammarian stands “bewildered and lost in thoughts”. Peter steps out of the boat, walks, sees the wind and begins to sink.

“Cast aside what thou hast learned … and cross the water!” Pope’s cure for the harm done by learning is more of it: a little is dangerous; drink deep. Is the grammarian’s fault that he has learned, or what he has learned to trust?
“Forsake thou every other concern … Confine thy thoughts.” The psalmist has narrowed his wants in the same way: one thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after.
“Independence of all things is as a door of guidance.” Thoreau, who had just decided not to buy a farm: a man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone.

The reading calls independence of all things a door. Whitman admires the animals for the same freedom, “not one is demented with the mania of owning things”, and equally because none kneels or discusses its duty to God. Is detachment a religious virtue, or older and plainer than religion?
“How pitiful it would be, were we to tarry, to hesitate.” A would-be follower asks leave to say farewell at home first, and is told about the plough.
This is the saying ‘Abdu’l-Bahá cites, taken here in a wider sense than a town that will not listen: to leave a place carrying nothing of it, not even the dust.

He accepted no gifts, “although on certain occasions we were in most straitened circumstances”. Confucius on coarse rice and water: riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness are to me as a floating cloud.

“We seek from you neither recompense nor thanks”, in a realm where “praise or blame can touch Him not”. Krishna teaches Arjuna the same freedom: let right deeds be thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them.

Bahá’u’lláh says that material relief was not refused, though His court is “sanctified from, and far above” such things. Agur’s prayer asks for the middle: neither poverty nor riches, lest either turn the heart. Is that moderation the same thing as detachment?
The joy of “these homeless wanderers” is in patience and detachment. Paul’s list of the apostles’ condition ends: as sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.
“Those who have renounced the world seek neither name nor fame.” The Sermon on the Mount forbids the commonest way of seeking them: alms done before men, to be seen.
“These to me are so many pebbles. The jewels I treasure are the jewels of the Knowledge of God.” The merchant of the parable sells every pearl he has for one.
“My happiness was perfect in those dark days of imprisonment.” Lovelace, from a London prison in 1642: stone walls do not a prison make, nor iron bars a cage.

“I was more happy then than now; because I had no will of my own. I was perfectly resigned.” Thoreau heard another thing under that word in his neighbours: what is called resignation is confirmed desperation. How is the one resignation told from the other?

“They whom neither merchandise nor traffic beguile from the remembrance of the Almighty”: the reading takes the phrase from this verse of the Qur’an, where it describes the houses in which the light is found.
“Blessed are the steadfastly enduring, they that are patient under ills and hardships.” James makes the same beatitude and names the pattern: ye have heard of the patience of Job.

Trials, says the reading, are “God’s method carried into effect of old”, and blessed are those “who lament not”. Ivan Karamazov finds the price of harmony too high and hastens to return his ticket. What would the reading have to say to him before asking for patience?

“Cleave tenaciously unto the cord of patience.” Shakespeare gives one of the best lines in praise of patience to Iago, who is using it to keep a dupe in hand. When is the counsel of patience to be trusted?
“Were it not for calamity, how would the sun of Thy patience shine?” Paul traces the growth: tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope.
“Be patient and grateful … Endeavour to become indifferent to the pleasures of this world.” Epictetus, once a slave: do not demand that things happen as you wish, but wish them to happen as they do.

“Such people have warrant over your bodies only, and God hath not reposed in them power over your spirits.” The Báb’s distinction is the Gospel’s: fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.
“To attain eternal happiness one must suffer.” The chorus of the Agamemnon credits Zeus with the same law: by affliction schooled, men learn, even against their will.
“Help me to be selfless at the heavenly entrance of Thy gate.” The psalmist would choose that place: I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God.
“Let the riches of Thine ancient countenance deliver me from all except Thee.” Thomas à Kempis amends the Preacher’s verdict by one clause: all is vanity, except to love God, and only to serve Him.

“Purify me of all that is not of Thee … that I may … be rid of all attachment.” Donne asks for the same thing with violence, knowing that he will not manage it himself: imprison me, for I never shall be free unless you enthrall me.

The prayer asks “so to surrender my will … that I may cease to discover within me any desire except what Thou didst desire”. Gethsemane shows the surrender while the desire is still there: not as I will, but as thou wilt.
“Any will save what Thou didst destine for me by Thy will.” Ignatius of Loyola’s prayer hands back liberty, memory, understanding and will together, and asks only for love and grace.
“Grant that I may die to all that I possess and live to whatsoever belongeth unto Thee.” Paul says that it has happened to him: I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.

The Fast is given so that souls may “rid themselves of all attachment to any one but Thee”. Isaiah’s chosen fast faces outward: to loose the bands of wickedness and deal bread to the hungry. Does detachment from all but God lead to the neighbour or away?
Set king over all realms, “my soul would still remain unsatisfied”. Augustine’s sentence is the best known form of the thought: our hearts are restless till they rest in You.
The prayer imagines having everything and finds it not enough. The Preacher tried it: whatever his eyes desired he kept not from them, and behold, all was vanity.
“Ignite … within my breast the fire of Thy love, that its flame may burn up all else.” The Song of Solomon says of love that its coals are coals of fire, which many waters cannot quench.

“Free me from the assaults of passion and desire, break off from me the shackles.” Augustine, asking for the same freedom, admits that it must be given: give what You command, and command what You will.

“I have severed every tie … except that most exalted tie that uniteth me with whosoever cleaveth unto Thee.” Told that his mother and brothers are outside, Jesus points to the disciples: whosoever shall do the will of my Father is my brother, and sister, and mother.
The one tie kept is the tie with those who cleave to God. The Qur’an lists the ties that compete with it, fathers, sons, clan, trade and dwellings, and tells those who hold them dearer to wait.

Every tie is severed here but one. Mencius thought a teaching that loosens the special claims of father and prince made men like beasts. What becomes of a parent’s or a ruler’s claim under the tie the prayer keeps?

Trials have encompassed the loved ones “for having renounced the world and set their affections on Thy realm of glory”. Paul weighs the two: our light affliction, which is but for a moment, against things not seen and eternal.

“Were I to inherit from Thee all the delights of Paradise … and … become, for less than a moment, careless of the remembrance of Thee, I would … cast them away.” Rābiʿa’s prayer gives away this world and the next on the same condition.
“Teach them to recognize the poverty of their own nature.” Paul is told, of the weakness he asked to be rid of: my strength is made perfect in weakness.
“A sense of their own powerlessness” is what the prayer asks for others. Bunyan’s shepherd boy sings of it as safety: he that is down needs fear no fall.
The speaker gives thanks “for having severed me from Thine enemies … and for having rid me of all attachment to them”. Paul asks for a like separation: what communion hath light with darkness?
The prayer asks that she “turn away from this mortal world of dust”. The Preacher’s first words: vanity of vanities; one generation passeth away, and another cometh.
“What will enable me to dispense with all except Thee.” The best known psalm begins there: the Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
“That which will make me independent of everyone else besides Thee.” The Qur’an records it said by people told that an army had gathered against them: Allah is sufficient for us.
“All else but Thee is in His eyes but a shadow.” Prospero on the towers, the palaces and the great globe itself: we are such stuff as dreams are made on.
“Aught save Thee is in His estimation but a handful of dust.” The Qur’an’s image for the life of the world is vegetation after rain, which pleases the farmer, yellows and becomes straw.
“Aid me to do what Thou desirest, and to fulfill what Thou pleasest.” The Lord’s Prayer: thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.

The prayer asks for “the living waters of Thy bounty, that they may rid him of all attachment to any one but Thee”. The water promised at the well does it by ending thirst: whoever drinks shall never thirst.
“Grant that I may, at all times and under all conditions, lay hold on Thy cord.” The Qur’an gives the image to a whole community: hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah.

“Ordain … for them what will make them rich enough to dispense with aught else except Thee.” Ben Zoma’s answer to who is rich is less absolute: he who rejoices in his lot. Is contentment with one’s portion the same wealth the prayer asks for?
Rich enough “to dispense with aught else”. Seneca defines poverty from the same side: it is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.

matthew-fear-not-them-which-kill.text: And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell

matthew-two-masters.text: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon

matthew-lilies-of-the-field.text: Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith

luke-rich-fool.text: And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God

luke-forsaketh-not-all.text: So likewise, whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple

luke-hand-to-the-plough.text: And another also said, Lord, I will follow thee; but let me first go bid them farewell, which are at home at my house. And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God

luke-one-thing-needful.text: Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her

mark-gain-the-whole-world.text: For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? Or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul

john-epistle-love-not-the-world.text: Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world. And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever

timothy-brought-nothing.text: For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out. And having food and raiment let us be therewith content. But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows

philippians-all-things-but-loss.text: But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ

galatians-yet-not-i.text: I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me

colossians-things-above.text: Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth. For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God

james-life-a-vapour.text: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain: Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away

james-patience-of-job.text: Take, my brethren, the prophets, who have spoken in the name of the Lord, for an example of suffering affliction, and of patience. Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy

psalm-vain-shew.text: Lord, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is: that I may know how frail I am. Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Selah. Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them

psalm-whom-have-i-in-heaven.text: Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever

psalm-one-thing-have-i-desired.text: One thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the Lord, and to enquire in his temple

psalm-wait-patiently.text: Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass

psalm-doorkeeper.text: For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness

psalm-number-our-days.text: The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away. Who knoweth the power of thine anger? even according to thy fear, so is thy wrath. So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom

ecclesiastes-vanity-of-vanities.text: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity. What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun? One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever

ecclesiastes-all-was-vanity.text: And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour: and this was my portion of all my labour. Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun

isaiah-wait-upon-the-lord.text: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint

lamentations-quietly-wait.text: The Lord is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him. It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord. It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth

corinthians-fashion-of-this-world.text: But this I say, brethren, the time is short: it remaineth, that both they that have wives be as though they had none; And they that weep, as though they wept not; and they that rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and they that buy, as though they possessed not; And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away

corinthians-having-nothing.text: As unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and, behold, we live; as chastened, and not killed; As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things

hebrews-moses-chose-affliction.text: By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter; Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season; Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward

hebrews-no-continuing-city.text: For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come

luke-possess-your-souls.text: In your patience possess ye your souls

matthew-treasure-hid-in-a-field.text: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field

proverbs-ruleth-his-spirit.text: He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city

proverbs-riches-make-wings.text: Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom. Wilt thou set thine eyes upon that which is not? for riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven

quran-play-and-pastime.text: Know that the life of the world is only play, and idle talk, and pageantry, and boasting among you, and rivalry in respect of wealth and children; as the likeness of vegetation after rain, whereof the growth is pleasing to the husbandman, but afterward it drieth up and thou seest it turning yellow, then it becometh straw. And in the Hereafter there is grievous punishment, and (also) forgiveness from Allah and His good pleasure, whereas the life of the world is but matter of illusion.

quran-comfort-of-illusion.text: Every soul will taste of death. And ye will be paid on the Day of Resurrection only that which ye have fairly earned. Whoso is removed from the Fire and is made to enter paradise, he indeed is triumphant. The life of this world is but comfort of illusion.

quran-life-as-water.text: And coin for them the similitude of the life of the world as water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingleth with it and then becometh dry twigs that the winds scatter. Allah is able to do all things.

quran-home-of-the-hereafter.text: This life of the world is but a pastime and a game. Lo! the home of the Hereafter - that is Life, if they but knew.

quran-dearer-than-allah.text: Say: If your fathers, and your sons, and your brethren, and your wives, and your tribe, and the wealth ye have acquired, and merchandise for which ye fear that there will no sale, and dwellings ye desire are dearer to you than Allah and His messenger and striving in His way: then wait till Allah bringeth His command to pass. Allah guideth not wrongdoing folk.

quran-with-the-steadfast.text: O ye who believe! Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast.

quran-neglect-not-thy-portion.text: But seek the abode of the Hereafter in that which Allah hath given thee and neglect not thy portion of the world, and be thou kind even as Allah hath been kind to thee, and seek not corruption in the earth; lo! Allah loveth not corrupters,

quran-grieve-not-nor-exult.text: That ye grieve not for the sake of that which hath escaped you, nor yet exult because of that which hath been given. Allah loveth not all prideful boasters,

quran-wasteth-away.text: That which ye have wasteth away, and that which Allah hath remaineth. And verily We shall pay those who are steadfast a recompense in proportion to the best of what they used to do.

quran-wealth-nor-children-distract.text: O ye who believe! Let not your wealth nor your children distract you from remembrance of Allah. Those who do so, they are the losers.

quran-living-and-dying-for-allah.text: Say: Lo! my worship and my sacrifice and my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the Worlds.

quran-love-of-joys.text: Beautified for mankind is love of the joys (that come) from women and offspring; and stored-up heaps of gold and silver, and horses branded (with their mark), and cattle and land. That is comfort of the life of the world. Allah! With Him is a more excellent abode.

gita-not-the-fruit.text: Find full reward / Of doing right in right! Let right deeds be / Thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them. / And live in action! Labour! Make thine acts / Thy piety, casting all self aside, / Contemning gain and merit; equable / In good or evil: equability / Is Yog, is piety!

dhammapada-give-up-what-is-before.text: Give up what is before, give up what is behind, give up what is in the middle, when thou goest to the other shore of existence

analects-bended-arm.text: With coarse rice to eat, with water to drink, and my bended arm for a pillow;-I have still joy in the midst of these things. Riches and honors acquired by unrighteousness, are to me as a floating cloud
analects-bended-arm.author: Confucius

avot-who-is-rich.text: Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32). Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot

rights.note: Translation published at Sefaria under a CC BY licence.

tagore-thousand-bonds-of-delight.text: Deliverance is not for me in renunciation. I feel the embrace of freedom in a thousand bonds of delight. Thou ever pourest for me the fresh draught of thy wine of various colours and fragrance, filling this earthen vessel to the brim. My world will light its hundred different lamps with thy flame and place them before the altar of thy temple
tagore-thousand-bonds-of-delight.author: Rabindranath Tagore

saadi-ten-dervishes.text: ten dervishes may sleep under the same blanket but that one country cannot hold two padshahs
saadi-ten-dervishes.author: Saʿdī

thoreau-afford-to-let-alone.text: a man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone
thoreau-afford-to-let-alone.author: Henry David Thoreau
thoreau-afford-to-let-alone.locator: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For

thoreau-quiet-desperation.text: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation. What is called resignation is confirmed desperation
thoreau-quiet-desperation.author: Henry David Thoreau

shakespeare-have-not-patience.text: How poor are they that have not patience! / What wound did ever heal but by degrees?
shakespeare-have-not-patience.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

whitman-live-with-animals.text: I think I could turn and live with animals, they are so placid and self-contain'd, / I stand and look at them long and long. / They do not sweat and whine about their condition, / They do not lie awake in the dark and weep for their sins, / They do not make me sick discussing their duty to God, / Not one is dissatisfied, not one is demented with the mania of owning things
whitman-live-with-animals.author: Walt Whitman

gray-paths-of-glory.text: The boast of heraldry, the pomp of pow'r, / And all that beauty, all that wealth e'er gave, / Awaits alike th'inevitable hour. / The paths of glory lead but to the grave
gray-paths-of-glory.author: Thomas Gray
gray-paths-of-glory.work: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard

epictetus-i-have-returned-it.text: Never say of anything, "I have lost it"; but, "I have returned it." Is your child dead? It is returned. Is your wife dead? She is returned. Is your estate taken away? Well, and is not that likewise returned?
epictetus-i-have-returned-it.author: Epictetus

kempis-vanity-except-to-love-god.text: Vanity of vanities, all is vanity, except to love God, and only to serve Him. This is the highest wisdom, by contempt of the world to tend towards the kingdom of Heaven
kempis-vanity-except-to-love-god.author: Thomas à Kempis

rights.note: Author d. 1471; an old English translation.

emerson-things-in-the-saddle.text: The horseman serves the horse, / The neatherd serves the neat, / The merchant serves the purse, / The eater serves his meat; / 'Tis the day of the chattel, / Web to weave, and corn to grind; / Things are in the saddle, / And ride mankind
emerson-things-in-the-saddle.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
emerson-things-in-the-saddle.work: Ode, Inscribed to W. H. Channing

seneca-craves-more.text: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor
seneca-craves-more.author: Seneca

rights.note: Published in the United States in 1917; translator d. 1969. One sentence.

bunyan-he-that-is-down.text: He that is down needs fear no fall / He that is low, no pride; / He that is humble ever shall / Have God to be his guide
bunyan-he-that-is-down.author: John Bunyan
bunyan-he-that-is-down.locator: Part II, the shepherd boy’s song
